results.content: AI in In-App Customer Complaints: Where Most Implementations Are Falling Short AI has become the default layer for customer support in consumer apps. Industry data suggests that nearly 90–95% of customer interactions are expected to involve AI, and a majority of enterprises are already using generative AI in support workflows. From a business lens, the intent is clear. → Reduce support costs. → Handle scale without proportional headcount. → Offer 24×7 availability. ⚠️ But the execution in many apps is often broken What customers experience: — Limited predefined options. — No way to explain context. — Poor continuity across interactions. — Human escalation that feels intentionally hard to reach. This isn’t an AI limitation. It’s an architecture and product design limitation. What many [...] an architecture and product design limitation. What many systems are doing today is decision-tree automation, not intelligent complaint handling. ——— Where the current AI support stack breaks: — Shallow NLP – intent detection without real contextual understanding. — No persistent memory – every interaction treated like a new ticket. — Binary escalation logic – rules-based handoff instead of confidence-based routing. — No sentiment awareness – frustration treated the same as a routine query. — AI optimised for deflection, not resolution. ——— AI can dramatically improve customer complaints when designed as an intelligence layer, not just a cost layer. A more robust approach should include: ✔ Free-text, LLM-driven intake. Let customers describe issues naturally. Modern LLMs can classify, [...] describe issues naturally. Modern LLMs can classify, summarise, and extract intent far better than forced menu flows. ✔ Context memory and state management. Maintain a complaint timeline across sessions. AI should know what was tried, what failed, and what’s pending. ✔ Confidence-based escalation. Use model confidence scores and sentiment signals to trigger human handoff automatically, before frustration peaks. ✔ Sentiment and emotion detection. Real-time tone analysis should dynamically adjust responses or escalate when emotional thresholds are crossed. ✔ Feedback-driven model retraining. Unresolved or escalated complaints should continuously improve the system. This is where most deployments fall short. ——— 🚀 AI done right doesn’t just lower costs. results.title: AI is wreaking havoc on mobile user experience, report finds
results.content:
### Dive Brief:

 AI-powered websites are frustrating mobile users due to broken elements and clunky interfaces, according to a report released Tuesday by Fullstory, a behavioral data company.
 Mobile error clicks skyrocketed 667% from 2024 to 2025, while mobile bounce rates increased 54%.
 The desktop user experience, on the other hand, has improved, as web error clicks fell 68% year over year. "Errors, rage clicks, and abandonments are far more common on mobile, with users hitting dead ends in nearly every visit," according to Fullstory.

### Dive Insight:

Rising user expectations, and their diminishing patience, is exacerbating mobile error clicks, especially as users grow accustomed to more efficient desktop AI interactions.

Login to comment [...] We believe a person's most valuable resources are their time, attention, presence, and focus. And we want sAVoR to be a tool that helps them cultivate those things and direct them to the arenas where they want them. One user might get a lot of satisfaction from getting through a lot of tasks, but another user may view their tasks as endless and want to just prioritize the ones they find essential (so that they can spend more time on their passion: swimming or crocheting or whatever it is).

A lot of productivity apps are designed to encourage more engagement, more activity, and more boxes checked. But we don't believe that being more productive necessarily means living a better or more fulfilling life. Sometimes the most valuable thing you can do is absolutely nothing on your to-do list.
